proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(s\in(1,2]\) and \(M\ge2\).  Choose
\[
 0<\varepsilon<\frac{1}{2(2+1/s)},
 \qquad
 \kappa_n=\frac18 n^{-\varepsilon},
 \qquad
 H_n=\left(\frac{\kappa_n}{2^{12}M}\right)^{1/s},
 \qquad c=\frac12,
\]
and write \(q_n=\kappa_n/H_n\).  Since \(s>1\),
\[
 q_n=(2^{12}M)^{1/s}\kappa_n^{\,1-1/s}\longrightarrow0. \tag{1}
\]
We now construct a full-data law.  Let \(X\) be uniform on \([0,1]\).  Conditional on \(X=x\), let the monotone response type \(R\) have probabilities
\[
 P_n(R=A\mid X=x)=\frac14,
 \qquad
 P_n(R=C\mid X=x)=w_n(x),
 \qquad
 P_n(R=N\mid X=x)=\frac34-w_n(x), \tag{2}
\]
where
\[
 w_n(x)=
 \begin{cases}
  \kappa_n,&x<c,\\
  \kappa_n+q_n(x-c),&x\ge c.
 \end{cases} \tag{3}
\]
By (1), \(0\le w_n(x)\le\kappa_n+q_n/2<1/4\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), so (2) consists of nonnegative masses summing to one.  Given \((X,R)\), take a Bernoulli random variable \(U\) of success probability \(1/2\), independent of \((X,R)\), and set
\[
 Y(0)=Y(1)=U. \tag{4}
\]
Use the threshold assignment \(Z=\mathbf 1\{X\ge c\}\) and the frozen monotone treatment rule \(D=D(Z)\), and take independent copies across units.

We verify membership in the frozen class.  From (2)--(3),
\[
 E_{P_n}[D(0)\mid X=x]=\frac14,
 \qquad
 E_{P_n}[D(1)\mid X=x]=\frac14+w_n(x). \tag{5}
\]
The two functions in (5) are continuous at \(c\), because both one-sided values of \(w_n\) there equal \(\kappa_n\).  By (4), \(E_{P_n}[Y(D(z))\mid X=x]=1/2\) for both \(z\), which verifies the required potential reduced-form continuity.  The observable treatment regressions are
\[
 \mu_{D,P_n}^{-}(x)=\frac14,
 \qquad
 \mu_{D,P_n}^{+}(x)=\frac14+\kappa_n+q_n(x-c). \tag{6}
\]
Thus the left regression has a constant extension and the right regression has the displayed affine extension to \([0,1]\).  Their suprema are bounded by one and their derivative suprema are at most \(q_n\); their derivative H\"older seminorms are zero.  Equation (1) and \(M\ge2\) therefore put both extensions in the radius-\(M\), order-\(s\) H\"older ball for all sufficiently large \(n\).  The two observable outcome regressions are the constant \(1/2\) and satisfy the same condition.  Moreover,
\[
 d_{P_n}=\mu_{D,P_n}^{+}(c)-\mu_{D,P_n}^{-}(c)=\kappa_n, \tag{7}
\]
so the strength shell holds.  Finally, (4) gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_n}(Y\mid X=x,\ell)=\frac14>v,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}_{P_n}(Y,D\mid X=x,\ell)=0 \tag{8}
\]
on either side \(\ell\).  Equations (2), (4)--(8), together with the uniform design, interior cutoff, and independent sampling, prove \(P_n\in\mathcal P_n(s,M,v,\kappa_n)\).

It remains to evaluate the population criterion induced by the profile construction.  For a candidate \(t\) with \(|t-c|\le H_n\), put
\[
 z=\frac{x-t}{H_n},
 \qquad
 r=\frac{c-t}{H_n},
 \qquad
 f_r(z)=\mathbf 1\{z\ge r\}(1+z-r). \tag{9}
\]
After subtracting the common affine function \(1/4\), (6) becomes \(\kappa_n f_r(z)\) on \([t-H_n,t+H_n]\).  For any prediction \(g\), the conditional squared-loss identity is
\[
 E_{P_n}[\{D-g(X)\}^2\mid X=x]
 =\operatorname{Var}_{P_n}(D\mid X=x)
  +\{\mu_{D,P_n}(x)-g(x)\}^2. \tag{10}
\]
The variance term in (10) is common to the affine and piecewise-affine fits and cancels from their risk difference.  The relevant least-squares coefficients are bounded uniformly for \(r\) in compact subsets of \((-1,1)\); after rescaling back to \(x\), their slopes are \(O(q_n)\) and their intercepts equal \(1/4+O(\kappa_n)\).  By (1), all these coefficients lie strictly inside the constraints in \(\mathrm{def:profile\mbox{-}cutoff\mbox{-}center}\) for large \(n\).  Hence those constraints do not alter the population projections used below.

Let \(Q_n(t)\) be population common-affine risk minus population piecewise-affine risk on \([t-H_n,t+H_n]\).  Uniformity of \(X\), (9), and (10) give
\[
 Q_n(t)=H_n\kappa_n^2 q(r), \tag{11}
\]
where direct projection on the bases \((1,z)\) over \([-1,1]\), \([-1,0]\), and \([0,1]\) gives
\[
 q(r)=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle
 \frac{(1+r)^2(7r^4-32r^3+27r^2+22r+4)}{24},&-1\le r\le0,\\[6pt]
 \displaystyle
 \frac{(1-r)^2(7r^4-52r^3+99r^2-10r+4)}{24},&0\le r\le1.
 \end{cases} \tag{12}
\]
For completeness, the common-affine Gram matrix in this calculation is
\[
 \int_{-1}^{1}
 \begin{pmatrix}1\\z\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}1&z\end{pmatrix}dz
 =\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2/3\end{pmatrix}, \tag{13}
\]
and the right-flank Gram matrix is
\[
 \int_0^1
 \begin{pmatrix}1\\z\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}1&z\end{pmatrix}dz
 =\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1/3\end{pmatrix}. \tag{14}
\]
Multiplying the moment vectors of \(f_r\) by the inverses of (13)--(14), and subtracting the two projection residuals, yields (12) equation by equation.

The formula has a strict displacement gain.  Indeed,
\[
 q(0)=\frac16,
 \qquad
 q\left(\frac25\right)=\frac{5949}{31250},
 \qquad
 \Delta:=q\left(\frac25\right)-q(0)=\frac{1111}{46875}>0. \tag{15}
\]
Also \(q(r)\le1/6\) whenever \(|r|\le1/8\).  To check the negative half, differentiation of the first polynomial in (12) gives
\[
 q'(r)=\frac{(1+r)(7r^4-22r^3+2r^2+20r+5)}4>0,
 \qquad -\frac18\le r\le0, \tag{16}
\]
because the parenthesized polynomial is at least \(5+20r\ge5/2\).  On the positive half, factorization gives
\[
 \frac16-q(r)
 =-\frac{r(r^2-4r+1)(7r^3-38r^2+51r-18)}{24}\ge0,
 \qquad 0\le r\le\frac18. \tag{17}
\]
Here \(r^2-4r+1>0\), while
\(7r^3-38r^2+51r-18\le7/512+51/8-18<0\), proving (17).

Let \(t_n^\circ=c-(2/5)H_n\).  The deterministic grid has mesh at most
\(\eta_n=\min\{n^{-1},m^{-1/3}H_n/64\}\), so it contains a point \(\bar t_n\) satisfying
\[
 |\bar t_n-t_n^\circ|\le\eta_n,
 \qquad
 \frac{\eta_n}{H_n}\le\frac{m^{-1/3}}{64}\longrightarrow0. \tag{18}
\]
Continuity of the polynomial in (12), (15), and (18) imply, eventually,
\[
 Q_n(\bar t_n)\ge H_n\kappa_n^2\left(\frac16+\frac{3\Delta}{4}\right),
 \qquad
 \sup_{|t-c|\le H_n/8}Q_n(t)\le\frac{H_n\kappa_n^2}{6}. \tag{19}
\]

We next compare the cross-fitted score with (11).  This step requires no extra law assumption.  The squared-loss classes in the construction are indexed by one interval endpoint and at most four affine coefficients in a fixed compact box.  Their envelopes are bounded by a constant depending only on \(M\).  For a sample of size \(m\), the interval endpoints induce at most a polynomial number of incidence patterns, and an \(m^{-3}\)-net of the compact coefficient boxes has polynomial cardinality.  Applying the elementary bounded exponential inequality to every element of this finite net and then using the Lipschitz dependence of squared loss on the coefficients yields, on each of the first three folds,
\[
 \sup_{t,g}\left|
  \frac1m\sum_{i\in F_j}\mathbf 1\{|X_i-t|\le H_n\}
       \{D_i-g(X_i)\}^2
  -E_{P_n}\!\left[\mathbf 1\{|X-t|\le H_n\}
       \{D-g(X)\}^2\right]
 \right|
 =O_{P_n}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right). \tag{20}
\]
The same finite-net argument applies separately to the two flank indicators.  Thus (20) is uniform over both the common and piecewise classes and over all candidate cutoffs; it also applies to a fitted function trained on another fold because the supremum is over every admissible coefficient vector.

Write the random bound in (20) as \(e_n\).  Empirical risk minimization and (20) imply, for either model class \(k\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
 0\le R_{n,t}^{k}(\widehat g_{j,t}^{k})
       -\inf_gR_{n,t}^{k}(g)\le2e_n. \tag{21}
\]
Applying (20) once more on the held-out fold and subtracting (21) for \(k=0,1\) gives
\[
 \sup_{t\in\mathcal T_n}|\widehat Q(t)-Q_n(t)|
 =O_{P_n}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right). \tag{22}
\]
By the choice of \(\varepsilon\),
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{\log n/n}}{H_n\kappa_n^2}
 =O\!\left(n^{-1/2+\varepsilon(2+1/s)}\sqrt{\log n}\right)
 \longrightarrow0. \tag{23}
\]
Combining (19), (22), and (23), with probability tending to one the score at \(\bar t_n\) is strictly larger than the score at every grid point in \([c-H_n/8,c+H_n/8]\).  Therefore the smallest maximizer \(\widetilde c\) in the construction satisfies
\[
 P_n\{|\widetilde c-c|>H_n/8\}\longrightarrow1. \tag{24}
\]

If the construction exits at the empirical-Gram check, it returns \(\mathsf F_{\mathrm{prof}}=1\), which is already counted on the left side of the claimed inequality.  Otherwise \(\widehat c_{\mathrm{prof}}=\widetilde c\); if the later fitted-jump check fails, it again sets \(\mathsf F_{\mathrm{prof}}=1\), and if that check passes then (24) places the returned center outside the radius \(H_n/8\).  Consequently,
\[
 P_n\{\mathsf F_{\mathrm{prof}}=1\}
 +P_n\bigl(\{|\widehat c_{\mathrm{prof}}-c|>H_n/8\}
       \cap\{\mathsf F_{\mathrm{prof}}=0\}\bigr)
 \longrightarrow1. \tag{25}
\]

Finally,
\[
 T_n=n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}
 =8^{-(2+1/s)}n^{\,1-\varepsilon(2+1/s)}, \tag{26}
\]
so \(T_n/\log(e/\kappa_n)\to\infty\).  Also \(nH_n\to\infty\), hence \(16/n\le H_n/8\) eventually.  For any fixed positive \(A_{\mathrm{prof}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{prof}}\), the proposed right side at \(u_n=H_n/8\) equals
\[
 A_{\mathrm{prof}}
 \exp\left\{-\frac{a_{\mathrm{prof}}m\kappa_n^2H_n}{8}\right\}
 =A_{\mathrm{prof}}
 \exp\left\{-\frac{a_{\mathrm{prof}}m}{8n(2^{12}M)^{1/s}}T_n\right\}
 \longrightarrow0, \tag{27}
\]
because \(m/n\to1/4\) and (26) diverges.  Equations (25) and (27) contradict the original positive claim for every choice of its three constants.  This proves the corrected negative statement.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Fix \(1<s\le 2\) and \(M\ge 2\).  The asserted uniform profile-localization inequality is false on \(\mathcal P_n(s,M,v,\kappa_n)\).  More precisely, there are a sequence \(\kappa_n\downarrow0\) and laws \(P=P_n\in\mathcal P_n(s,M,v,\kappa_n)\), all with \(c_P=1/2\), for which
\[
 \frac{T_n}{\log(e/\kappa_n)}\longrightarrow\infty
\]
but, on putting \(H_n=(\kappa_n/(2^{12}M))^{1/s}\) and \(u_n=H_n/8\), one has \(16/n\le u_n\le H_n\) eventually and
\[
 P_n\{\mathsf F_{\mathrm{prof}}=1\}
 +P_n\bigl(\{|\widehat c_{\mathrm{prof}}-c_{P_n}|>u_n\}
          \cap\{\mathsf F_{\mathrm{prof}}=0\}\bigr)
 \longrightarrow1.
\]
Consequently, no positive constants \(A_{\mathrm{prof}},a_{\mathrm{prof}},C_{\mathrm{prof}}\), depending only on \(s,M\), can satisfy the displayed conclusion in the original statement.  The obstruction is an admissible mismatch of the two one-sided derivatives: for the moving-window common-versus-piecewise affine score, it moves the population maximizer a fixed fraction of \(H_n\) away from the actual jump.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The moving-window profile is not centered at the true cutoff under the frozen class. An admissible one-sided derivative mismatch of size \(\kappa_n/H_n\) produces the exact rescaled profile in the proof; its population score at displacement \(2H_n/5\) exceeds its score throughout the \(H_n/8\)-neighborhood of the cutoff. The empirical cross-fitted score converges uniformly fast enough along the displayed strong-signal sequence, so the claimed exponential localization bound is false. The proposed statement records the resulting negative theorem without strengthening or substituting the model class.
